messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Vignette:
Amara was seventy-four years old when the rape happened, though she still speaks of it as though it were last week. She had worked the same stretch of farmland outside a small Georgia town for nearly forty years, rising before dawn to tend rows of collards, okra, and sweet potatoes. The memory that haunts her begins on a late October evening, just after dusk, when she stayed later than usual to finish harvesting pumpkins for a local market. The air smelled of turned earth and damp leaves—a scent she had always associated with peace, with the end of a good day. That evening, a man came out of the darkness near the equipment shed. He grabbed her, pressed her face into the soil, and raped her while the last light faded. She remembered trying to scream, but the only sound was the rustle of dry grass and then, after he left, a silence so total she thought she had gone deaf. The silence felt worse than the pain; it felt like the world had erased her.

In the weeks that followed, Amara tried to push the memory away. She told herself she had to think only good things—how her grandchildren laughed, how the sun felt on her back, how her partner, Marcus, still brought her sweet tea every evening. She forced a smile when neighbors asked how she was, and she repeated the positive thoughts like a prayer until her jaw ached. But the strategy only worked for minutes at a time. The smell of soil would drift up from a turned garden row, and suddenly she was back on the ground, the weight of the man crushing her chest. She would freeze, then hurry to the far end of the field, but the smell followed her. She began to dread the simple act of walking to her toolshed. On the anniversary, exactly one year later, she stayed inside all day, but the memory arrived anyway, unbidden, like a guest she could not turn away.

What frightened Amara most was not the memory itself but the lasting stain she felt on her skin. She washed three, four times a day, scrubbing until her hands were raw. She believed she was permanently soiled, that her body had been made filthy in a way that could never be cleaned. Whenever Marcus reached for her hand or touched her shoulder, she flinched, and she saw hurt flicker across his face. She started sleeping on the far edge of their bed, avoiding any contact, because being touched made her feel the dirt all over again. She began to refuse his goodnight kiss, then stopped sitting next to him on the porch. Marcus asked what was wrong, and she said “nothing” because she could not tell him the truth—that she felt ashamed of what had happened to her body, as though it were her fault for being in the dark, for staying too late, for being a woman alone in the field.

To avoid the dark, she rearranged her whole life. She stopped working the early morning shifts that had once been her favorite, when the stars were still out and the dew made everything quiet. She insisted on finishing all outdoor tasks before sunset, even if it meant leaving crops unharvested. At home, she kept every light on until she fell into exhausted sleep. The silence that followed the rape became another trigger; sudden quiet in the house—when Marcus turned off the television or the refrigerator hum stopped—would make her heart race. She started keeping a radio on at all times, just to fill the air with noise.

Months passed, and Amara’s world grew small. She was still working the fields, but she moved slower, avoided certain patches of earth, and flinched if a coworker came too close. Her boss noticed, but she waved him off. She felt increasingly certain that her life was not worth living anymore, though she never said it aloud. What finally brought her to seek help was Marcus finding her one evening, sitting in the bathroom with the shower running, staring at her hands and crying. He said he was scared for her, and she realized she was scared too. She came to the clinic because she was tired of feeling dirty in her own skin, and because she could not bear the thought of losing the only person who still reached for her—even if she still could not let herself be touched. She hopes, more than anything, to feel clean again.
